title: Git Internals: Disjoint Sets
description: Merge tracking with Union-Find data structures

content.overview: Disjoint-set data structures (also known as Union-Find) are used to track sets of elements partitioned into non-overlapping subsets. In Git, similar concepts are used for efficient merge tracking and conflict resolution. This module explores how Git uses disjoint-set-like structures to manage branches and merges.

steps.title: Understanding Disjoint Sets
steps.content: A disjoint-set data structure maintains a collection of disjoint (non-overlapping) sets. It provides operations to add new sets, merge existing sets, and determine which set an element belongs to.

steps.title: Union-Find Operations
steps.content: The Union-Find data structure supports three main operations: MakeSet (create a new set), Find (determine which set an element belongs to), and Union (merge two sets).

Are A and C connected? true

behindTheCommand.title: Optimizing Union-Find
behindTheCommand.content:
Two key optimizations make Union-Find operations very efficient:

1. **Path Compression**: During Find operations, make each node on the path point directly to the root, flattening the tree structure
2. **Union by Rank**: When merging sets, attach the smaller tree to the root of the larger tree to minimize tree height

With these optimizations, operations become nearly constant time (technically O(α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function, which grows extremely slowly).

steps.title: Disjoint Sets in Git's Merge Tracking
steps.content: Git uses concepts similar to disjoint sets to track which branches have been merged and which commits are reachable from different branches.

behindTheCommand.title: Git's Commit Reachability
behindTheCommand.content:
Git needs to efficiently determine which commits are reachable from which branches. This is conceptually similar to the connected() operation in Union-Find:

1. **Branch Tracking**: Git tracks which branches have been fully merged into others
2. **Commit Reachability**: Git determines if a commit is an ancestor of another commit
3. **Merge-Base Finding**: Git finds the best common ancestor of two commits

These operations are essential for merge operations, branch management, and determining which commits to push or fetch.

steps.title: Conflict Resolution with Disjoint Sets
steps.content: When merging branches, Git needs to determine which changes conflict and which can be automatically merged. Disjoint-set-like structures help track which parts of files have been modified by different branches.

behindTheCommand.title: Three-Way Merge Algorithm
behindTheCommand.content:
Git's merge algorithm uses a three-way merge approach that conceptually relates to disjoint sets:

1. **Common Ancestor**: Find the merge base (common ancestor) of the two branches
2. **Change Sets**: Identify changes made in each branch relative to the common ancestor
3. **Disjoint Changes**: Changes to different parts of the file can be automatically merged
4. **Overlapping Changes**: Changes to the same parts of the file result in conflicts

This approach allows Git to automatically merge non-conflicting changes while identifying conflicts that require manual resolution.
